catalog_quote: Written accents practically played no part in either Vulgar Latin or Old French. In this grammar they are used to mark stress. ... It is not necessary to mark the stress of Old French words, for the primary stress may be placed by an inviolable rule — on the ultima unless the ultima vowel be § [scanned glyph for Luquiens' feminine-e symbol e̥], in that case on the penult — and the secondary stress (79. Note) is not of great importance. We therefore use acute accents over Old French words for a special purpose — to mark that one of the vowels of a diphthong or triphthong which has the greater force : for instance, Old French veiture is stressed on the penult, but the e of the diphthong of the antepenult is pronounced more forcibly than the i. ... sweep_summary: Old French (oldf1239) is in the catalog as 'weight' (stress final unless the final vowel is schwa, then penult), deciding source Luquiens 1909. The title search returned four Glottolog items, all Benjamins publications. (1) Morin 1991 'Old French Stress Patterns and Closed Syllable Adjustment' (CILT 69: 49-76) is squarely about Old French word stress and stress-conditioned vowel reduction (per Rainsford 2011 pp. 38-39, which reports Morin's Hebrew-gloss evidence and his suggestion that reduction was never conditioned purely by primary-stress position); it is paywalled with no open copy or abstract anywhere I could reach — highest acquisition priority. (2) Jacobs 1992 (CILT 74: 55-80; Glottolog dates it 1991) treats Latin-to-Old-French foot structure and, per Rainsford 2011 p. 190, proposes at p. 68 that schwa is extrametrical — a formalization of the catalog's rule; paywalled, medium priority. (3) Jacobs 1991 'Old French Proclisis and Enclisis' (Linguistics in the Netherlands 8: 91-100) is CC BY-NC open access; downloaded, converted and read in full: it is about clitic-attachment domains (clitic group vs Prosodic Word) and never states where word stress falls — silent on the classification, no priority. (4) Callahan 1984 (CILT 26: 343-354) concerns prosodic domains of assimilation rules, not stress placement; paywalled, low priority. No works with stress in the title contradicts the classification. 63 (open access, held by the project since the 9/16 check), which states the final-unless-schwa rule with IPA examples and, together with Rainsford 2011 p. 33 (quoting Pope 1952 sec. 223), is a better deciding citation than Luquiens 1909. txt added; written).

new_statements.quote: Lexical stress in Old French (9th–13th century) shows a simple surface pattern: it is final (1a), except where the final vowel is a schwa, in which case it is penultimate (1b): (1) a. petit [pə.ˈtit] 'small.' b. ensemble [ẽn.ˈsẽm.blə] 'together'. In one sense, this surface pattern persists until the apocope of final schwa at the end of the 16th century, when stress becomes regularly word-final.
new_statements.citation: Rainsford, Thomas M. 2020. Syllable structure and prosodic words in Early Old French. Papers in Historical Phonology 5: 63-89. doi:10.2218/pihph.5.2020.4433 (open access, CC BY)
new_statements.reading: Stress is on the last syllable unless that syllable's vowel is schwa, in which case it is on the penult — exactly the catalog's right-edge full-vs-reduced-vowel ('weight') coding and Luquiens 1909's rule. Caveat on provenance: this statement was downloaded and recorded in the 2026-09-16 check pass, and I re-read it from disk in this search of works with stress in the title; none of the four title-works with stress in the title yielded a first-hand stress-placement statement (Jacobs 1991 AVT is the only one obtainable and is silent; Morin 1991, Jacobs 1992, Callahan 1984 are paywalled). The layer drops the fi-ligature ('inal'); the quote restores 'final' as printed. Rainsford 2011 thesis p. 33 (p. 49) states the same rule in a boxed 'MedFr stress rule' and quotes Pope 1952 sec. 223.

sources.citation: Rainsford, Thomas M. 2020. Syllable structure and prosodic words in Early Old French. Papers in Historical Phonology 5: 63-89. doi:10.2218/pihph.5.2020.4433 (open access)
sources.quote: 'Lexical stress in Old French (9th-13th century) shows a simple surface pattern: it is final (1a), except where the final vowel is a schwa, in which case it is penultimate (1b): petit [pə.ˈtit], ensemble [ẽn.ˈsẽm.blə].' Develops Jacobs (1994) analysis that the rule is underlyingly a right-aligned trochee with final stress arising from an empty-headed final syllable — a formal refinement consistent with our right-edge, full-vs-reduced-vowel coding.
sources.locator: p. 63 (p. 1), sec. 1 Introduction, ex. (1a-b); analysis pp. 79-80
sources.note: Peer-reviewed open-access phonology article whose first sentence states the Old French lexical stress rule with IPA examples; gives a formal (trochaic/empty-nucleus) analysis relevant to the 'weight'/full-vs-reduced-vowel classification.

sources.citation: Rainsford, Thomas M. 2011. The Emergence of Group Stress in Medieval French. PhD thesis, University of Cambridge (St John's College). 300 pp. doi:10.17863/CAM.16503
sources.quote: 'MedFr stress rule: Stress the final syllable of the word, unless the vowel in that syllable is a schwa, in which case stress the penult.' ... 'the primary stress in MedFr fell on exactly the same syllable of the word as it had done in vulgar Latin (Pope, 1952: sec. 215)'. Fn. 22: Pope (1952: sec. 223): 'Old French [was] a language in which all words were oxytone or paroxytone, and, if paroxytone, then always ending in a syllable containing /ə/.' Thesis further argues group (phrase-final) stress develops mid-12th to mid-13th c., layered on this word-stress rule.
sources.locator: Ch. 1 sec. 3 'Stress-related phenomena in medieval French', printed p. 33 (p. 49), boxed 'MedFr stress rule'; fn. 22 quoting Pope 1952 sec. 223
sources.note: The only full-length modern study of medieval French stress; states the word-stress rule explicitly (p. 33) and dates the shift toward group stress — replaces a 1909 student handbook as primary citation.

sources.citation: Jacobs, Haike. 1991. Old French Proclisis and Enclisis: The Clitic Group or the Prosodic Word? Linguistics in the Netherlands 8: 91-100. doi:10.1075/avt.8.12jac (CC BY-NC 4.0).
sources.quote: In Old French, monosyllabic unstressed words could be pronounced either as part of the word that preceded them (enclisis), as in, for instance, jot vi 'I saw (perf.) you', or as part of the word that followed them (proclisis), as in, for example, Erec m'apelent 'They call me Erec.' ... The particular focus of this paper is the domain within which Old French enclisis and proclisis applied.
sources.locator: p. 91, sec. 0 Introduction (p. 1); p. 93 for the De Kok quotation
sources.note: Read in full (10 pp.). The paper is about the prosodic domain of Old French clitic attachment (enclisis jot vi / proclisis Erec m'apelent), arguing against Nespor & Vogel's clitic group and for Selkirk's end-based Prosodic Word with parameter setting {Right, Lex0}. It refers to 'monosyllabic unstressed words' and to clitics attached to 'un mot pleinement accentue qui precede' (De Kok 1985, quoted p. 93) but contains no statement of where word stress falls in Old French polysyllables; stress readjustment is discussed only for Modern Greek examples. Silent on the catalog's classification.
